title.en: A pinch of salt that shook an empire

text.en: In 1930 a small, thin man walked for 24 days to a beach and picked up a pinch of salt. That act defied a mighty empire. We follow how Indians came together against British rule.

The First World War created new economic and political problems: heavy defence expenditure, price rise and forced recruitment of soldiers, so people were ready to protest.
Mahatma Gandhi returned from South Africa in 1915 and led satyagraha in Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad. In 1919 he called a nationwide satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act.
On 13 April 1919 General Dyer's troops fired on a peaceful crowd at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, killing hundreds and shaking the country.
The Non-Cooperation Movement began in 1920 with the Khilafat issue. People gave up titles, boycotted schools, courts and foreign cloth. It was called off after violence at Chauri Chaura in 1922.
The Simon Commission of 1927 had no Indian members. In December 1929 the Lahore Congress under Jawaharlal Nehru demanded Purna Swaraj, complete independence.
The Salt March began on 12 March 1930 from Sabarmati and reached Dandi on 6 April, where Gandhi broke the salt law. It launched the Civil Disobedience Movement.
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact of 1931 ended the movement for a time. The Poona Pact of 1932 gave depressed classes reserved seats in provincial councils after the dispute with Ambedkar.
The sense of collective belonging grew through history, folklore, songs, the image of Bharat Mata and flags. Different groups understood freedom in their own ways.

problem.en: How many years passed between Jallianwala Bagh (1919) and the Salt March (1930)?

prompt.en: Describe the role of Gandhi's satyagraha in the freedom struggle.

requiredIdeas.en: Mass participation in Champaran, Rowlatt and Salt

points.en: WWI hardships and Rowlatt Act led to protests.
Non-Cooperation (1920-22) and Civil Disobedience (1930) were mass movements.
Purna Swaraj was demanded at Lahore in 1929.
